extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in marketing history and corporate scandals
extracted.subtask_description: A popular-press retrospective recounting the 1985 'New Coke' product change, its causes, consumer reaction, and lasting lessons about branding and corporate decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for changing the Coca-Cola recipe
rubrics_metrics.description: Coca‑Cola cited a lethargic cola market, a dip in consumer awareness and preference, and a slipping share lead over PepsiCo as reasons to change the formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The company presented these market indicators as justification for reformulating; decision-makers should document market trends (awareness, preference, share) that motivate product reformulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on taste-test results
rubrics_metrics.description: Company-reported taste tests indicated nearly 200,000 consumers preferred the taste of New Coke over old Coke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using taste-test data as a primary decision lever can be persuasive but risky — the article highlights that prioritizing taste-test outcomes without accounting for other factors (like legacy) was later judged to be a key mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of brand legacy and emotional attachment
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece emphasizes the 'passion for original Coca‑Cola' — an emotional, hard-to-measure attachment consumers had to the original formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of product changes should account for intangible consumer attachments (pride, patriotism, nostalgia) that standard metrics may not capture; quotes note 'you cannot measure it any more than you can measure love, pride or patriotism.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer backlash as a metric of failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate and measurable consumer reactions included tripled hotline calls, stockpiling of the old formula, protest signs ('We want the real thing'), letters insulting executives, and songs lamenting the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor indicators of consumer anger or refusal (consumer service volume, protests, hoarding, grassroots campaigns) as evidence of negative reception; these can drive rapid corporate reversals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of product change and speed of reversal
rubrics_metrics.description: New Coke's 'reign' lasted only 79 days before the company restored the original formula as Coca‑Cola Classic and sold both alongside each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A very short time between launch and reversal is an implicit metric of strategic failure; longevity and market acceptance over time are critical success measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal framing of the initiative as strategic risk-taking
rubrics_metrics.description: Company leadership later described New Coke as an 'intelligent risk' that signaled willingness to do what was necessary to build value for owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating such initiatives, weigh intended strategic aims (market-dynamics change, shareholder value) against brand and consumer costs; post-hoc framing by executives may recast failures as deliberate experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing conspiracy vs. explained motive (need for fact-checking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some theorized New Coke was a ploy to boost the original product; fact‑checking (Snopes) calls that theory false and instead points to misprioritizing taste tests over legacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sensational explanations against evidence and reputable fact-checks; distinguish between intentional marketing ploys and genuine strategic errors based on documented motives and data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of nostalgia and later promotional revivals
rubrics_metrics.description: New Coke later resurfaced in limited runs (e.g., 2019 Stranger Things promotion) and Coca‑Cola repackaged variants (Coke II) before pulling them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A failed product can be monetized later via nostalgia/limited promotions, but such revivals do not negate initial strategic missteps; consider long-term brand equity effects when relaunching legacy products.
